source.title: Measuring Feature Sparsity in Language Models
source.authors: Mingyang Deng; Lucas Tao; Joe Benton

record.tranche_reason: The study measures sparse feature decompositions in language-model activations, extending sparse-feature claims from toy settings to language models with different metrics.
record.gate_note: The paper validates its metrics on synthetic sparse and non-sparse data, but does not train or test toy networks for superposition geometry. Those results do not test V1. The study's feature examples are qualitative; numerical sparsity values appear in figures, while the text reports the comparisons and trends.
record.test_reason: The study applies sparse coding to activations of real language models (BERT, TinyStories, GPT-Neo/GPT-2) and measures whether they are well modelled as sparse linear combinations of dictionary features, against non-sparse controls. This is a new setting with results bearing on V4. It does not train toy networks or examine superposition geometry, so V1 is not tested. Its synthetic experiments only validate the metrics.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that activations across the tested architectures and all layers are sparser than control datasets, supporting the linearity and sparsity hypotheses, with sparsity greatest in the first (embedding) and final layers.
record.recipe_differences: The study develops normalized-loss and average-coefficient metrics and applies sparse coding to language-model activations; it does not reproduce the original toy-model method or test its superposition geometry.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported sparsity trend changes with layer depth: it decreases at first and increases again in the latest layers. The paper also reports that BERT representations are slightly sparser than TinyStories representations.
record.problems: The evidence is indirect: normalized loss is a proxy for sparsity, and the study does not establish that recovered components are complete or canonical features. Several quantitative results are available only in figures; uncertainty estimates are not stated.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant results left out. Synthetic metric-validation results test the measurement metrics on generated data, not toy-network superposition.

untested.parts: No toy networks are trained. Overlap and near-orthogonality, the sparsity-dependent transition and regular geometry are not examined.
Capacity or importance as the cause of polysemanticity is not tested.
Alternative causes of polysemanticity are not tested.
Whether features are spread across many neurons (neuron-level polysemanticity) is not measured. Only sparse-dictionary recoverability is measured.
Completeness, stability and canonicity of the dictionary features are not tested.
1-D and multi-dimensional features are not compared.

missing.what: Variance explained by the sparse decompositions: over 90% for token embeddings across all models, and at least 98% for every BERT model and layer (Fig. 3b). This bears on how well the dictionary recovers activations.
The average-coefficient-norm metric gives results 'very similar' to normalized loss, for embeddings (Fig. 9) and across layers (Fig. 10). This is a robustness check on the V4 rows.
missing.locator: Appendix F Fig. 9; Appendix H Fig. 10

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. Its evidence for V4 is indirect: normalized loss is a proxy validated on synthetic data. Separation from controls is clear, but numerical values are figure-only and no uncertainty is reported. The dictionary is overcomplete (8d–16d). The models are small; the largest named is TinyStories 33M, and the GPT-2 sizes are unstated.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test learned toy networks, feature overlap or near-orthogonality, a sparsity-dependent transition, or regular superposition geometry.
Does not test whether capacity pressure causes polysemanticity or whether feature importance determines dedicated versus shared dimensions.
Does not test alternative causes of polysemantic neurons or whether polysemanticity occurs without capacity pressure.
Tests sparse linear decompositions and feature examples in selected language models, but not whether features are spread across many neurons. It uses sparse coding, not an SAE specifically.
Does not test whether dictionary features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
Uses vector features in its sparse-coding setup but does not compare one-dimensional features with multidimensional features.

rows.subject: BERT Tiny
rows.operation_detail: Sparse-code activations from Wikipedia abstracts across layers.
rows.measure: Normalized loss as a proxy for sparsity; trend across layer depth
rows.value: All layers are described as sparse; the general trend is lower sparsity with increasing depth followed by greater sparsity in the latest layers.
rows.note: The trend is stated across the four BERT models; individual layer values are plotted.
rows.check: The baseline is left as 'not stated'. The Gaussian and other control datasets are the implied comparison: the conclusion says all layers are 'more sparse than several control datasets'. The sparsity decoding λ was set per model (0.0027–0.01), so cross-model comparison depends on that choice.

source_check.correct: The concluding comparison is against several control datasets, rather than no stated baseline. Section 4.2 reports sparse activations in all layers, with sparsity generally decreasing from embeddings before increasing in the latest layers. Appendix H specifies a 16d dictionary, training λ=0.1 and decomposition λ=0.0027 for BERT Tiny.
source_check.locator_found: Section 4.2, Figure 3 discussion; Section 5, opening paragraph; Appendix H, lines 606–611.
source_check.problem: The baseline omits the control-dataset comparison stated in the conclusion.

rows.subject: GPT-2
rows.operation_detail: Decompose the token embedding into sparse-coded feature components and inspect maximally activating examples.
rows.measure: Qualitative coherence of top feature components
rows.baseline: Closest embedding directions for comparison are described as more polysemantic
rows.value: The top three components are interpreted as TV/radio shows, yearly seasons, and lengths of time.
rows.note: The authors say the maximally activating examples suggest natural interpretations.
rows.check: The evidence is qualitative only: two hand-picked tokens with authors' interpretations. The baseline is Table 3, the nearest embedding neighbours, which the authors call more polysemantic.

rows.subject: GPT-2
rows.operation_detail: Decompose the token embedding into sparse-coded feature components and inspect maximally activating examples.
rows.measure: Qualitative coherence of top feature components
rows.value: The top three components are interpreted as physical sciences, fields of study, and astronomy.
rows.note: The authors say the maximally activating examples suggest natural interpretations.
rows.check: The evidence is qualitative and hand-picked, with no baseline comparison for physics.

relation.reason: Its own sparse-coding measurements and control comparisons assess whether language-model activations admit sparse linear feature decompositions.

tranche.reason: The study tests sparse linear representations in real language-model embeddings and later-layer activations, extending the toy-model setting with results bearing on V4.

source_check.notes: The authors' conclusion is accurately paraphrased. Exact Figure 2 values are unavailable in the extracted text; qualitative examples are hand-picked, and the control comparison for later layers is stated in the conclusion rather than plotted as a per-layer baseline.

statements.correction: Appendix H: at least 98% activation variance explained for every tested layer of BERT Tiny, Mini, Small and Medium on Wikipedia abstracts; dictionary size 16d; training λ=0.1; decomposition λ=0.0027, 0.0037, 0.0047 and 0.01 respectively. The paper identifies itself as a preprint and reports synthetic control datasets.
